hints: Calculate the maximum limiting friction on $Q$ using $R_Q = 0.1g\cos 60^\circ = 0.5\text{ N}$ and $F_{\text{max}} = \mu R_Q = 0.35\text{ N}$.
Calculate the net gravitational force attempting to move the system along the string: $0.2g\sin 60^\circ - 0.1g\sin 60^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \approx 0.866\text{ N}$.
Compare the net driving force with the maximum friction: since $0.866\text{ N} > 0.35\text{ N}$, conclude that the particles move.
walkthrough:
Calculate the normal reaction and maximum limiting friction acting on particle $Q$:
$$R_Q = 0.1g\cos 60^\circ = 0.1(10)(0.5) = 0.5\text{ N}$$
$$F_{\text{max}} = \mu R_Q = 0.7 \times 0.5 = 0.35\text{ N}$$

Calculate the net gravitational pulling force along the string before friction acts:
$$F_{\text{drive}} = 0.2g\sin 60^\circ - 0.1g\sin 60^\circ = 2\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) - 1\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \approx 0.866\text{ N}$$

Compare the driving force with maximum friction and conclude:
$$F_{\text{drive}} - F_{\text{max}} = 0.866 - 0.35 = 0.516\text{ N} > 0$$
$$\text{Since the driving force exceeds the maximum friction force, the particles move.}$$

ai_rubric.Using Limiting Equilibrium: Calculates R_Q = 0.5 N, maximum friction = 0.35 N, net driving force = 0.866 N, and concludes particles move.

teacher_walkthrough: Identify the potential direction of motion: particle $P$ has greater mass ($0.2\text{ kg}$) than $Q$ ($0.1\text{ kg}$) on identical $60^\circ$ slopes, so $P$ tends to move downwards, pulling $Q$ upwards.

Find the normal reaction force $R_Q$ on the rough slope supporting particle $Q$:
$$R_Q = m_Q g\cos 60^\circ = (0.1)(10)(0.5) = 0.5\text{ N}$$

Calculate the maximum possible friction force opposing the motion of $Q$ using $F_{\text{max}} = \mu R_Q$:
$$F_{\text{max}} = 0.7 \times 0.5 = 0.35\text{ N}$$

Calculate the components of weight parallel to the slope for both particles:
$$\text{For } P:\quad W_{P,\parallel} = 0.2g\sin 60^\circ = 2\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = \sqrt{3} \approx 1.732\text{ N}$$
$$\text{For } Q:\quad W_{Q,\parallel} = 0.1g\sin 60^\circ = 1\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \approx 0.866\text{ N}$$

Find the net force driving the system before friction is considered:
$$F_{\text{drive}} = W_{P,\parallel} - W_{Q,\parallel} = \sqrt{3} - \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \approx 0.866\text{ N}$$

Compare the net driving force with the maximum available friction:
$$F_{\text{drive}} - F_{\text{max}} = 0.866 - 0.35 = 0.516\text{ N} > 0$$
$$\text{Because the net gravitational force }(0.866\text{ N})\text{ strictly exceeds the maximum friction }(0.35\text{ N}),\text{ the particles move.}$$

hints: Apply Newton's second law to particle $P$ along its slope: $0.2g\sin 60^\circ - T = 0.2a$.
Substitute $T = \sqrt{3} - 1\text{ N}$ and solve for the common acceleration $a = 5\text{ m s}^{-2}$.
Apply Newton's second law to particle $Q$ moving up its smooth slope: $T - 0.1g\sin\theta = 0.1a$.
Substitute $T = \sqrt{3} - 1$ and $a = 5$ to find $\sin\theta = \sqrt{3} - 1.5$, then evaluate $\theta$.
walkthrough:
Apply Newton's second law to particle $P$ moving down the smooth $60^\circ$ slope:
$$m_P g\sin 60^\circ - T = m_P a$$
$$0.2(10)\sin 60^\circ - (\sqrt{3} - 1) = 0.2a$$
$$\sqrt{3} - \sqrt{3} + 1 = 0.2a \implies 0.2a = 1 \implies a = 5\text{ m s}^{-2}$$

Apply Newton's second law to particle $Q$ moving up the smooth slope inclined at $\theta$:
$$T - m_Q g\sin\theta = m_Q a$$
$$(\sqrt{3} - 1) - 0.1(10)\sin\theta = 0.1(5)$$
$$(\sqrt{3} - 1) - \sin\theta = 0.5$$

Solve for $\sin\theta$ and calculate the angle $\theta$:
$$\sin\theta = \sqrt{3} - 1.5 \approx 0.23205$$
$$\theta = \sin^{-1}(0.23205) \approx 13.4^\circ$$

ai_rubric.Solving Connected-Particle Systems: Solves 0.2g sin 60 - (sqrt(3) - 1) = 0.2a for a = 5 m s^-2, and (sqrt(3) - 1) - 0.1g sin theta = 0.1(5) for theta = 13.4 deg.

teacher_walkthrough:
Apply Newton's second law $F_{\text{net}} = ma$ to particle $P$ ($0.2\text{ kg}$) moving down its smooth $60^\circ$ incline:
$$m_P g\sin 60^\circ - T = m_P a$$

Substitute the given tension $T = \sqrt{3} - 1\text{ N}$, $m_P = 0.2\text{ kg}$, and $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$:
$$(0.2)(10)\sin 60^\circ - (\sqrt{3} - 1) = 0.2a$$
$$2\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) - \sqrt{3} + 1 = 0.2a$$
$$\sqrt{3} - \sqrt{3} + 1 = 0.2a$$
$$1 = 0.2a$$

Divide both sides by $0.2$ to solve for acceleration:
$$a = \frac{1}{0.2} = 5\text{ m s}^{-2}$$

Apply Newton's second law to particle $Q$ ($0.1\text{ kg}$) accelerating up its smooth incline at angle $\theta$ with the same acceleration $a = 5\text{ m s}^{-2}$:
$$T - m_Q g\sin\theta = m_Q a$$

Substitute $T = \sqrt{3} - 1\text{ N}$, $m_Q = 0.1\text{ kg}$, $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$, and $a = 5\text{ m s}^{-2}$:
$$(\sqrt{3} - 1) - (0.1)(10)\sin\theta = (0.1)(5)$$
$$(\sqrt{3} - 1) - \sin\theta = 0.5$$

Evaluate numerically and find the angle:
$$\sin\theta \approx 1.732051 - 1.5 = 0.232051$$
$$\theta = \sin^{-1}(0.232051) \approx 13.4178^\circ$$
$$\theta = 13.4^\circ\quad (\text{to 3 significant figures})$$
